The Haber process is the industrial way of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen, worked out in Germany in 1909. The chemist Fritz Haber made it work in the laboratory, and Carl Bosch of the chemical company BASF turned it into a factory process, with the first plant running in 1913.

Plants need nitrogen to grow, and before this farmers got extra nitrogen mainly from manure, Chilean saltpetre and seabird droppings shipped from Peru in the Guano Era. The Haber process made nitrogen fertiliser cheap and almost unlimited.

  • In the First World War it let Germany make explosives even after the British blockade cut off Chilean nitrate.
  • After 1945 it fed the huge rise in crop yields that culminated in the Green Revolution.
  • Today about half the world's people are fed by food grown with this nitrogen.

The process has costs. It runs on hydrogen made mostly from natural gas, so it burns a lot of fossil fuel, and fertiliser washing off fields pollutes rivers and coastal seas. Haber himself won the Nobel Prize in 1918 but also led Germany's poison gas program in the First World War, which makes him one of the most mixed figures in the history of science.
